answer.rationale: With the contract lapsing in 14 days and the line running at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, switching primary vendors (memory_c2) carries onboarding and integration risk that could jeopardize delivery continuity right when there's no slack to absorb disruption. Renewing incumbent as-is (memory_c1) preserves stability but doesn't address the 18% cost mandate. Negotiating terms at renewal (memory_c4) has precedent for recovering real margin while keeping the same stable integration, directly serving the TCO-minimization objective without introducing a new-vendor risk during a volume-constrained period. I verified memory_c4 to confirm the renegotiation record reflects genuine, repeatable savings rather than a one-off concession, and memory_c2 to check whether the low-cost vendor switch's 'quick onboarding' claim holds under tight timelines, since that risk directly bears on the current 14-day deadline. Given only single-cycle data points behind each memory, I'm treating the cost-savings magnitudes as directional rather than guaranteed, and flagging that squeezing margin from the incumbent could still indirectly affect service scope or responsiveness later, which needs monitoring next cycle.
